The Throughline

This trip loosely follows the final chapter of the Apostle Paul's life — his shipwreck on Malta (Acts 27–28), his path through Sicily and the Bay of Naples, and his imprisonment and death in Rome — layered over three civilizations' worth of history: Phoenician, Greek, Roman, Baroque, and modern.

Back to Top
02 · Paul's Journey & the Early Church›
The Throughline

Paul's Journey & the Early Church

This is the spine the whole trip hangs on. Every stop that follows — Malta, Sicily, Naples, Rome — is a scene in the same story: a small, contested, barely-organized movement finding its footing, one shipwreck and one house church at a time. Worth reading this before the cities, not after — it changes what you're looking at once you're standing in front of it.

"The Way" — Before It Was Called ChristianityActs 9, 19, 24›

In the Book of Acts, Paul's movement is repeatedly called "the Way" (Greek hodos) — not a new religion, but a renewal movement inside Judaism, centered on the claim that Jesus of Nazareth was the promised Messiah. Paul himself, before his conversion, describes persecuting "the Way" (Acts 9:1–2), traveling to Damascus specifically to arrest its followers. The word "Christian" only shows up later, first coined (possibly as an outsider's nickname) in Antioch, in modern Turkey (Acts 11:26). For the movement's first few decades, its members were still worshipping in synagogues, still keeping Jewish feast days, still thinking of themselves as Jews who believed the Messiah had already come.

That matters for how you read this trip: Paul's shipwreck in Malta, his journey to Rome, his death there — all of it happens while the movement is still small, contested, and largely indistinguishable to Roman authorities from any other Jewish sect.

The Viper on MaltaActs 28:1–6›

The morning after the shipwreck, cold and soaked, Paul is gathering brushwood for a fire when a viper, driven out by the heat, latches onto his hand. The islanders watching — Acts calls them simply "the natives," genuinely kind, building the fire and sharing what they had — immediately assume he's a murderer, someone the sea itself failed to kill and justice was now finishing off. When Paul calmly shakes the snake into the fire and doesn't swell up or drop dead, they flip completely: now he must be a god.

It's a small, strange story, but it's the actual origin point of Malta's centuries-long devotional relationship with Paul — the shipwreck church, the grotto in Rabat, the whole island's sense of itself as "Paul's island" traces back to these few verses. Worth having in your head walking into St. Paul's Shipwreck Church on Sep 10.

Why Rome? Paul's Own LogicRomans 1, Acts 28›

Paul wrote to the Roman church years before he ever set foot there: "I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome" (Romans 1:15) — he saw Rome not as a detour but as a strategic endpoint, the administrative center of the entire empire his message was spreading through. Acts ends (28:30–31) with Paul under house arrest in Rome for two years, "proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance" — and then the narrative simply stops. Tradition, not scripture, fills in the rest: his release, further travel, a second arrest, and execution under Nero, likely around AD 64–68.

The logic was structural: Rome's roads and sea lanes, built for legions and tax collectors, worked just as well for missionaries. A message that could take root in the capital could, in theory, spread along every route the empire had already paved.

The Prison EpistlesPhilippians, Colossians, Ephesians, Philemon›

Those two years of house arrest in Rome (Acts 28:30) weren't idle time. Tradition holds Paul wrote at least four surviving letters from custody there — Philippians, Colossians, Ephesians, and the short, personal note to Philemon — collectively "the Prison Epistles." Some of the most quoted lines in the New Testament come from this stretch, written under guard, possibly in a rented house near where you'll be walking: "I can do all things through him who strengthens me" (Philippians 4:13); "To live is Christ, and to die is gain" (Philippians 1:21).

2 Timothy, written later and under harsher conditions during what tradition holds was a second, final imprisonment, reads very differently — more urgent, more personal, clearly a man aware he's near the end. That's the letter believed written from the Mamertine Prison itself, on your Sep 16 stop.

House Churches, Not BuildingsNo dedicated church buildings for 200+ years›

There was no such thing as a purpose-built church for roughly the first two centuries of the movement. Early Christians met in private homes, in borrowed rooms, sometimes in the courtyards of wealthier converts who could host a few dozen people. It's part of why the movement was so hard for Roman authorities to track or suppress cleanly — there was no single building to close down, no registry of members, just a loose network of households. When you visit grand basilicas like St. John Lateran (dedicated AD 324) or St. Peter's, you're seeing what happened only after Christianity became legal and, later, the state religion — architecture catching up to a movement that had already been alive for three centuries without it.

Nero and the Fire of RomeAD 64 · Tacitus, Annals XV›

In July AD 64, a fire tore through Rome for six days, destroying much of the city. The Roman historian Tacitus, writing decades later, records that Emperor Nero — facing rumors he'd started the fire himself to clear land for a new palace — shifted blame onto Christians, a small and already unpopular group. Tacitus describes brutal executions that followed: Christians "torn by dogs," others "nailed to crosses," some "set on fire to serve as torches" for nighttime entertainment in Nero's own gardens.

Tradition holds that both Peter and Paul were executed in Rome during this general period — Peter reportedly crucified upside down (by his own request, considering himself unworthy to die as Christ did), Paul beheaded, since Roman citizens were legally exempt from crucifixion. Neither death is described in the New Testament itself; both accounts come from later Christian tradition, which is exactly why the trip treats sites like the Mamertine Prison and the Abbey of Tre Fontane as traditional, not certain, locations.

Two Apostles, One CityFeast of Sts. Peter & Paul, June 29›

Peter and Paul make an odd pair to end up venerated together: Peter, the uneducated Galilean fisherman, apostle to the Jews, one of the original twelve who actually walked with Jesus; Paul, the trained Pharisee and Roman citizen, apostle to the Gentiles, who never met Jesus before the resurrection and spent his early years persecuting the church Peter helped lead. Different backgrounds, reportedly real tension between them at points (Paul describes confronting Peter directly in Galatians 2), yet tradition holds both died in Rome under Nero within the same general period, and the church has honored them jointly since antiquity — June 29 is still the Feast of Saints Peter and Paul, a public holiday in Rome.

The city's two great basilicas mark the symmetry: St. Peter's over his traditional burial site on the Vatican Hill, St. Paul Outside the Walls over his on the opposite side of the city — both stops on this trip, bookending Rome the way the two apostles bookend the New Testament's early history.

The Catacombs — Myth vs. RealityCatacombs of St. Sebastian, Sep 17›

A popular myth (helped along by old Hollywood films) says Christians dug the catacombs to hide from persecution underground. That's mostly false. Roman law simply prohibited burial within the city walls, for any religion, so everyone's cemeteries sat outside them — the catacombs were legal, known burial complexes, not secret hideouts. Christians used them because underground tunneling was cheaper than surface land near the city, and because the dead of a tight-knit community could be buried together. Some persecuted Christians likely did meet there for services or funerals in relative privacy, but "secret refuge" is an exaggeration of a real, permitted practice. After Christianity was legalized, the catacombs became pilgrimage sites in their own right — people wanted to be buried near early martyrs, a practice that continued for centuries after the original persecutions ended.

From Underground Movement to State ReligionEdict of Milan, AD 313›

The turning point came in AD 313, when Emperor Constantine and his co-emperor Licinius issued the Edict of Milan, legalizing Christianity across the empire after roughly 250 years of intermittent, sometimes brutal persecution. Constantine's own conversion (traditionally linked to a vision before the Battle of the Milvian Bridge, AD 312) reshaped the empire's relationship to the faith almost overnight. Within a decade, Constantine was funding major church construction, including St. John Lateran, dedicated in AD 324 as Rome's cathedral — the very first stop on your Rome itinerary.

By the end of the 4th century, under Emperor Theodosius, Christianity became the empire's official state religion. The arc is genuinely dramatic: a persecuted house-church movement, meeting in secret and burying its dead outside the walls, became within roughly 300 years the religion of the empire that once fed its followers to lions. You're visiting sites from both ends of that story on this trip — the Mamertine Prison and the catacombs from the persecution era, St. John Lateran and St. Peter's from the triumph that followed.

Malta's whole identity is "crossroads." Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Romans, Arabs, Normans, the Knights of St. John (Hospitallers), the French, and the British all held it in turn. The Pauline angle is central here: Acts 27–28 describes Paul's shipwreck around AD 60.

Valletta — Sep 10

  • Grand Master's PalaceHQ of the Knights of St. John, 1571–80s. Armoury, tapestried State Rooms.
  • St. Paul's Shipwreck ChurchSpecial-permit visit; relic of the column of Paul's beheading.
  • St. John's Co-CathedralBaroque showstopper. Two Caravaggios, including his largest and only signed work.
  • Upper Barrakka GardensGrand Harbour views; noon cannon salute.

Festival Note

The Valletta International Guitar Festival runs Sep 10–12, 2026 — classical, flamenco, and jazz guitar in historic venues around the city, right on your Malta nights.

Mdina & Rabat — Sep 11

  • MdinaThe car-free "Silent City," former capital. Traditional site of Paul meeting governor Publius.
  • Domus Romana1st-century Roman townhouse, mosaics, just outside Mdina's walls.
  • St. Paul's Grotto (Rabat)Pilgrimage site since antiquity; visited by two popes.
  • San Pawl MilqiRoman villa tied to Paul's first reception on the island.

Weather & Logistics

  • Still warm — 28–30°C days, sea at its warmest.
  • Sep 8 is Victory Day, a Malta public holiday, just ahead of the trip.

The Ferry Crossing

The Malta–Pozzallo ferry roughly retraces the ancient shipping lane Paul himself sailed (Acts 28: Malta → Syracuse → Rhegium → Puteoli). A 3am wake-up, but a full day still ahead on landing.

Syracuse (Siracusa)

  • Neapolis Archaeological ParkGreek Theatre (5th c. BC) and the Ear of Dionysius, a cave named by Caravaggio for its shape and acoustics.
  • Ortigia & the DuomoA cathedral built around the columns of a 5th-century BC Temple of Athena.
  • Fountain of ArethusaA couple minutes from the Duomo — a rare freshwater spring bubbling up at the sea's edge. Greek myth: the nymph Arethusa fled the river god Alpheus and was turned into this spring by Artemis.
  • Caravaggio's Burial of St. LucySanta Lucia alla Badia, on Piazza del Duomo. Painted 1608, right after Caravaggio fled prison in Malta — the next chapter of the same fugitive story.

Archimedes of Syracuse

Born and lived here (c. 287–212 BC). Source of "Eureka!" and the buoyancy principle that bears his name; built war machines to defend the city against the besieging Roman fleet. Killed during the Roman sack despite General Marcellus's orders to spare him — supposedly absorbed in a geometry problem when a soldier struck him down.

Taormina

  • Teatro AnticoGreek foundations, Roman rebuild. Mount Etna smoking through the stage arches.
  • Still an active concert venue — don't be surprised by stage equipment even off-hours.
  • CannoliNon-negotiable here. Get one filled to order, not pre-filled, so the shell stays crisp.

Overnight in the Messina area, an ancient Greek colony and the traditional gateway to mainland Italy.

Try seltz al limone from a street kiosk — fresh lemon, soda water, a pinch of salt. A different, more old-school tradition than a lemonade stand.

Buried by pyroclastic flow rather than ash — paradoxically better-preserved organic material than Pompeii, and far fewer crowds.

Naples Museum & Montecassino

Antica Pizzeria Da Michele — the pizza pilgrimage, if there's a window near the museum. Operating since 1870, widely credited as the birthplace of modern Neapolitan pizza. Just two options: margherita or marinara. A short taxi ride, not walkable.

Beyond the Official Itinerary — A Caravaggio Trail

The fugitive story that started in Malta (Sep 10) and continued in Syracuse (Sep 12) finishes here. Nothing below is official, but it clusters tightly around stops you already have.

Near Piazza Navona · Sep 15

  • The LeonardoVatican Pinacoteca, Room IX — St. Jerome in the Wilderness, the only da Vinci painting in Rome. Some tours skip the Pinacoteca; worth asking the guide.
  • The Momo StaircaseOn the way out of the Vatican Museums — the famous double-helix spiral, a 1930s tribute to Bramante's 1505 original. Time your exit for a photo straight down.
  • Sant'AgostinoMinutes from Piazza Navona. Caravaggio's Madonna di Loreto and Raphael's Prophet Isaiah fresco, painted right after the Sistine ceiling was unveiled.
  • Via della ScrofaThe walk from Sant'Agostino to San Luigi — Caravaggio's actual neighborhood, and where his real trouble started (a fight with a notary, precursor to the killing that got him exiled — the whole reason he ends up in Malta and Sicily).
  • San Luigi dei FrancesiThe full "St. Matthew Cycle," three Caravaggios in one chapel. Free, but bring a euro coin for the lights.
  • Cerasi Chapel, Santa Maria del PopoloFurther north. Two more Caravaggios facing each other: Crucifixion of St. Peter and Conversion of St. Paul.
  • Spanish Steps10–15 min from Piazza del Popolo, or tack onto Ara Pacis. 135 steps, 1723–25. The fountain at the base is by Bernini's father — same family as the Four Rivers Fountain.

Near the Colosseum · Sep 16

  • Michelangelo's MosesSan Pietro in Vincoli, short walk from the Colosseum/Forum. Famous for its small horns — a translation quirk from Hebrew "rays of light."
  • The TabulariumUnderneath the Senatorial Palace, Capitoline Hill. Ancient Rome's state archive (78 BC), Doric arches opening onto the Forum. Needs a Capitoline Museums ticket.

● · The Artists›
Bonus Track

The Artists

Caravaggio gets his own trail because his story runs the length of the trip. These five worked in the same rooms, sometimes the same decade — tap any name for background before you're standing in front of the work.

Michelangelo Buonarroti1475–1564 · Sistine Chapel, Pietà, Moses›

Born in Caprese, apprenticed to Ghirlandaio at 13, then taken in by Lorenzo de' Medici's household in Florence, where he studied ancient sculpture alongside the Medici family's own children. He thought of himself as a sculptor, not a painter, and said so loudly — which makes the Sistine Chapel commission (1508) something close to an insult, forced on him by Pope Julius II. He initially refused, then relented, then fired his assistants and painted almost the entire 12,000-square-foot ceiling himself, lying on his back on custom scaffolding for four years. He wrote a poem to a friend about the physical toll: his beard pointed at the ceiling, paint dripping into his eyes, his spine bent out of shape.

The Last Judgment on the altar wall came 25 years later (1536–41), commissioned by a different pope after the 1527 Sack of Rome — noticeably darker and more anguished than the ceiling, painted by a man in his 60s who had lived through the city's worst trauma in a century.

His Pietà, carved at just 24 for a French cardinal, sits inside St. Peter's entrance — his only signed work, after he reportedly overheard someone attribute it to another sculptor and snuck back at night to carve his name across the sash. His Moses (San Pietro in Vincoli) was meant for an enormous 40-plus-statue tomb for Julius II that never got finished; Michelangelo called the project "the tragedy of the tomb." In his final years, he became chief architect of St. Peter's Basilica and designed its dome — completed after his death, largely to his design.

Raphael (Raffaello Sanzio)1483–1520 · School of Athens, Isaiah, his own tomb›

Born in Urbino, trained under Perugino, in Rome by 25 and immediately put to work frescoing the papal apartments — the Raphael Rooms — while Michelangelo was simultaneously up on scaffolding a few hundred feet away painting the Sistine ceiling. The two barely spoke; contemporaries describe real rivalry. The School of Athens, his masterpiece in the Stanza della Segnatura, is a who's-who of ancient philosophy: Plato and Aristotle centered, Plato pointing up toward abstract forms, Aristotle gesturing down toward the physical world. Faces throughout are modeled on Raphael's own contemporaries — Leonardo as Plato, Michelangelo added late as a brooding Heraclitus after Raphael reportedly snuck a look at the half-finished Sistine ceiling, and Raphael himself tucked into the corner as a self-portrait.

His Prophet Isaiah fresco at Sant'Agostino (1511–12) was painted in the same spirit — a deliberate homage to Michelangelo's style, done so well that some contemporaries assumed Michelangelo had secretly coached him.

He died suddenly at 37, on his birthday, after a short fever — Vasari's gossipy account blames a night with his mistress followed by concealing the resulting illness from his doctors. Uniquely among the artists on this trip, you can visit his grave: he's buried inside the Pantheon, already on your Sep 15 itinerary. His tomb bears a line written by his friend Cardinal Bembo: "Here lies Raphael, by whom Nature herself feared to be outdone."

Gian Lorenzo Bernini1598–1680 · St. Peter's colonnade, Four Rivers Fountain›

Born in Naples, a genuine child prodigy — carving marble portrait busts by his teens that impressed Pope Paul V. He went on to dominate Roman art and architecture for over 50 years, favored by eight consecutive popes, essentially designing the public face of Baroque Rome. His sweeping colonnade around St. Peter's Square (1656–67) was meant, in his own words, to embrace visitors "like the maternal arms of Mother Church." Inside, his bronze baldachin over the high altar stands seven stories tall, cast partly from bronze stripped from the Pantheon's portico — a detail that scandalized Romans at the time.

The Fountain of the Four Rivers in Piazza Navona (1651) personifies four continents' great rivers — the Nile, Ganges, Danube, and Río de la Plata — around an Egyptian obelisk. Legend says one figure shields its eyes from the facade of a rival architect's nearby church, though the timeline makes that a later invention, not fact.

His personal life had real scandal: a passionate affair with Costanza Bonarelli, the wife of one of his assistants, ended when Bernini discovered she was also involved with his own brother — he had her face slashed with a razor by a servant in retaliation. The Pope fined him and quietly arranged his marriage to someone else shortly after. None of it slowed his career.

Leonardo da Vinci1452–1519 · St. Jerome in the Wilderness›

By the time Leonardo reached Rome in 1513, at 61, he was already the most famous artist in Italy — and increasingly a man out of step with the city's mood. Pope Leo X's court was consumed with Michelangelo and the fast-rising Raphael, both younger, both faster, both hungrier for the huge fresco commissions Leonardo had once defined. He was given rooms in the Vatican's Belvedere and a stipend, but little serious painting work; contemporaries describe him spending his three Roman years largely on scientific studies — anatomy, optics, mechanical designs — rather than canvases.

St. Jerome in the Wilderness, the unfinished painting now in the Vatican Pinacoteca, actually predates this period by about 30 years (c. 1480–82) — abandoned mid-work, the underdrawing still visible. It vanished for centuries and turned up in the 1800s literally cut into pieces: the head was being used as a stool seat, the rest as a cobbler's workbench, before Napoleon's uncle tracked down and reassembled every fragment.

Frustrated in Rome, Leonardo left in 1516 for France at the invitation of King Francis I, who gave him a manor house and a title, "First Painter, Engineer, and Architect to the King," and reportedly just wanted him nearby to talk to. He died there in 1519 — Vasari's famous, likely embellished account has him dying in the king's arms.

Donato Bramante1444–1514 · Belvedere Courtyard, the original spiral staircase›

The oldest of this group and, in a sense, the one who made room for the others. Trained originally in Urbino and Milan, Bramante arrived in Rome in his 50s and was appointed by Pope Julius II as chief architect of a project bigger than anything in the city: a completely new St. Peter's Basilica, replacing Constantine's 1,100-year-old original. His plan was a Greek cross under a massive central dome, directly inspired by the Pantheon he studied nearby — a design later modified by successors, Michelangelo among them, who took over the dome decades after Bramante's death.

Critics nicknamed him "Bramante Ruinante" — Bramante the Ruiner — for how readily he demolished old Rome to build the new: chunks of Old St. Peter's, ancient churches, medieval neighborhoods, all cleared to make way. His Belvedere Courtyard (1505), a massive terraced garden connecting the Vatican Palace to a hillside villa, included a spiral ramp inside its tower designed so Pope Julius II could ride a horse straight up to his apartments — the direct inspiration for the double-helix Momo Staircase you'll walk past leaving the Vatican Museums today.

He died in 1514, only the foundations and a few piers of the new St. Peter's built. Everything that followed — Raphael's brief tenure as architect, then Michelangelo's dome — built on his foundation, literally.

08 · Research Notes›
Section 08

Research Notes & Rabbit Holes

Caravaggio

Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio (1571–1610) is directly relevant to two stops. At St. John's Co-Cathedral, his Beheading of Saint John the Baptist (1608) is his largest surviving work and the only one he signed — in the pooling blood. He painted it as a fugitive, having fled Rome after killing a man in 1606; the Knights made him a Knight of Grace, then defrocked him in the same room about six months later, as a "foul and rotten member."

The cathedral's second Caravaggio, Saint Jerome Writing, was stolen from that exact room on New Year's Eve 1984 and recovered nearly two years later — told in full in PBS's The Caravaggio Heist (2021) and Fr. Marius Zerafa's Caravaggio Diaries.

His Rome breakout came earlier: the Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi (1599–1600), a short walk from Piazza Navona — worth a detour if there's a free window on Sep 15.

The Great Siege of 1565 & Victory Day ✓ researched

Malta's Sep 8 public holiday commemorates the Knights' defense against a massive Ottoman invasion fleet in 1565. Knight Ippolito Malaspina arrived with the relief force at the siege's climax; his relative Vespasianus Malaspina died defending Fort St. Elmo and is memorialized inside St. John's Co-Cathedral itself.

09 · Glossary›
Section 09

Art & Architecture Glossary

Style Terms

  • Baroque(c. 1600–1750) — drama, gold, intense light/dark contrast. Nearly everything in Malta and Rome.
  • TenebrismExtreme chiaroscuro; figures spotlit against near-black backgrounds. Caravaggio's signature.
  • Renaissance(c. 1400–1600) — restrained, mathematically balanced. Sistine ceiling and Raphael Rooms.
  • Basilica planLong rectangular hall, rounded apse, borrowed from Roman civic buildings.

Masters on Your Path

  • MichelangeloSistine ceiling (1508–12); the Pietà, carved at 24.
  • BerniniSt. Peter's Square colonnade; the Four Rivers Fountain.
  • RaphaelThe Raphael Rooms, including The School of Athens.
  • Mattia PretiPainted the ceiling and gilding inside St. John's Co-Cathedral.
Don't walk past: the Pietà, The School of Athens, the Four Rivers Fountain, The Beheading, and the Alexander Mosaic.

11 · Field Notes›
Section 11

Field Notes & Practicalities

The Tour, Officially

  • Tour hostPastor Steve Kellar, traveling with the group.
  • OperatorTutku Travel — official start is Malta arrivals hall, Sep 10, where a rep holds a "STEVE KELLAR – TUTKU" sign after customs/baggage claim, then private bus transfer to the hotel.
  • English-speaking assistantwith the group Sep 10–14; local guides (2–8 hrs/day per program) join for each city after that.
  • Whisper headsetsprovided for the Italy portion of the trip (12 days).

Hotels

  • Malta (2 nights)Hotel Cavalieri or similar.
  • Taormina area (1 night)Hotel Capo dei Greci or similar.
  • Pompeii (1 night)Hotel Palma or similar.
  • Rome (4 nights)Best Western Hotel Universo or similar.

Worth Knowing

  • Malta & Sicily: 27–30°C, still swim-worthy sea. Rome cools slightly mid-month.
  • Catania–Naples leg is Ryanair — 1 checked bag (20kg), 1 carry-on (10kg), plus 1 small personal item.
  • Sep 11 in Malta includes a second, exterior-only stop at St. Paul's Bay to see the Shipwreck Church from outside — different from the special-permit interior visit on Sep 10.
  • Sep 13's lunch (Herculaneum) is included and specifically built around Neapolitan pizza — the tour's own nod to "pizza where it was invented," ahead of whatever you do in Naples proper.
  • Sep 16: the Palatine Hill is admired from Capitoline Hill on this itinerary, not entered directly — worth knowing so you're not looking for a separate ticket line.
  • Most lunches are on your own (one exception: the included Pompeii-day lunch); drinks, tips to drivers/guides, and porterage are also not included in the tour price.
Packing — Maurice Moves
Watch"How to Pack ONE BAG for a Vacation" — Maurice's core approach: a handful of high-quality, versatile pieces that layer well, weigh less, and stay fresh longer, over a big pile of options. Useful given how much walking and how many hotel changes this trip has (7 different beds in 9 nights).
